title: Color-Emotion Associations and Color Preferences: A Case Study for Residences
abstract: This study investigated color-emotion associations and color preferences in residences using 41 color samples and 30 adjectives with 50 participants. Results showed a strong dependency between the choice and use of green at residences. Emotional responses to colors were found to change with value and saturation levels. Gender and age were identified as determining factors in the selection of achromatic black.
introduction: Color is an important design element that can meet a variety of human needs. Past research indicates that individuals associate colors with emotions, and color preferences are influenced by linguistic, cultural, age, gender, and background factors. The study aims to observe color-emotion associations and discuss why and how certain colors are selected for specific interior spaces in residences.
methodology: Fifty Turkish volunteers (30 female, 20 male, mean age 32, range 18-65) participated. Participants had no theoretical or practical knowledge about color and no color blindness. The study used 41 color samples from a popular Turkish color producer's catalogue (RAL system based). Participants were tested individually under controlled environmental conditions (200 lx incandescent lamps, CRI 1A). The procedure involved two steps: 1) matching 30 adjectives (positive, negative, non-emotion) with color samples, and 2) offering color samples for various residence areas (living/dining, kitchen, bathroom, bedroom, children's bedroom, corridor, entrance, stair hall), categorized by activity, required emotion, and proposed color.
results: Emotional responses to colors varied across hues, values, and saturations. Green, pink, and yellow frequently evoked positive emotions like excitement, cheerfulness, and warmth, while green and blue were associated with calmness and relaxation. Green was also linked to negative emotions like boredom and depression. Black showed a strong dependency on age (P = 0.029) and gender (P = 0.031), with all participants aged 63+ preferring black, and all females expressing positive emotions towards black. For residence interiors, a strong dependency was found only for green (P = 0.043), with pale, low-saturation green samples favored. Pink was preferred for sleeping and children's rooms, blue for living rooms, and yellow for dining areas. Near-white, green, blue, and yellow were suggested for hygiene-focused areas like kitchens and bathrooms.
discussion: Color-emotion associations are subjective and influenced by personal like-dislikes, previous knowledge, and experience. Different color samples can evoke the same emotional response, and a single adjective can be matched to multiple colors. Changes in value and saturation levels of a hue significantly influence emotional associations, more so than the hue itself. The finding that females had positive emotional responses to black contradicts some previous research. The contradiction regarding green (eliciting both positive and negative emotions but being preferred for dwellings) warrants further investigation into the role of tints and shades. Cross-cultural studies and evaluations of designers' preferences are suggested for future research.

limitations: Color samples were unspecified in previous universal scale of color preference studies.
Age range was not identified in previous universal scale of color preference studies.
No quantitative analysis of lightness and chroma at hue angle 0° was performed.
Low frequency of responses for some color chips, tints, and shades led to grouping under same hue category.
The study was based on end-user preferences in Turkey, limiting cross-cultural generalizability.
Contradiction between green eliciting depression and being offered for dwellings needs further examination of tints and shades.
